entries.e4cf312e4538cdc53b0303a2ef49b6dedee5de1b: <div sID="gen13259" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="147" osisID="Ps.147" sID="Ps.147"/> <div eID="gen13259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13260" type="x-p"/> This is another psalm of praise. Some think it was penned after the return of the Jews from their captivity; but it is so much of a piece with <reference osisRef="Ps.145.1-Ps.145.21">Ps. cxlv.</reference> that I rather think it was penned by David, and what is said (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.2">ver. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.13">13</reference>) may well enough be applied to the first building and fortifying of Jerusalem in his time, and the gathering in of those that had been out-casts in Saul's time. The Septuagint divides it into two; and we may divide it into the first and second part, but both of the same import. I. We are called upon to praise God, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.12">12</reference>. II. We are furnished with matter for praise, for God is to be glorified, 1. As the God of nature, and so he is very great, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.4-Ps.147.5 Ps.147.8 Ps.147.9 Ps.147.15-Ps.147.18">ver. 4, 5, 8, 9, 15-18</reference>. 2. As the God of grace, comforting his people, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.3">ver. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.10">10,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.11">11</reference>. 3. As the God of Israel, Jerusalem, and Zion, settling their civil state (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.2">ver. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.13">13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.14">14</reference>), and especially settling religion among them, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.19-Ps.147.20">ver. 19, 20</reference>. It is easy, in singing this psalm, to apply it to ourselves, both as to personal and national mercies, were it but as easy to do so with suitable affections.
entries.1b1b27058bd734e01630114fd626b882f86545be: <div eID="gen13260" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Call to Praise God; Reasons for Praise.</title> <div sID="gen13261" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for <hi type="italic">it is</hi> good to sing praises unto our God; for <hi type="italic">it is</hi> pleasant; <hi type="italic">and</hi> praise is comely. 2 The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> doth build up Jerusalem: he gathereth together the outcasts of Israel. <hi type="super">3</hi> He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds. <hi type="super">4</hi> He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by <hi type="italic">their</hi> names. <hi type="super">5</hi> Great <hi type="italic">is</hi> our Lord, and of great power: his understanding <hi type="italic">is</hi> infinite. <hi type="super">6</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> lifteth up the meek: he casteth the wicked down to the ground. <hi type="super">7</hi> Sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with thanksgiving; sing praise upon the harp unto our God: <hi type="super">8</hi> Who covereth the heaven with clouds, who prepareth rain for the earth, who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains. <hi type="super">9</hi> He giveth to the beast his food, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to the young ravens which cry. <hi type="super">10</hi> He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man. 11 The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> taketh pleasure in them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy. <div eID="gen13261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13262" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The duty of praise is recommended to us. It is not without reason that we are thus called to it again and again: <hi type="italic">Praise you the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.1">v. 1</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.7">v. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Sing unto the Lord with thanksgiving, sing praise upon the harp to our God</hi> (let all our praises be directed to him and centre in him), <hi type="italic">for it is good</hi> to do so; it is our duty, and therefore good in itself; it is our interest, and therefore good for us. It is acceptable to our Creator and it answers the end of our creation. The law for it is holy, just, and good; the practice of it will turn to a good account. It is good, for 1. It is pleasant. Holy joy or delight are required as the principle of it, and that is pleasant to us as men; giving glory to God is the design and business of it, and that is pleasant to us as saints that are devoted to his honour. Praising God is work that is its own wages; it is heaven upon earth; it is what we should be in as in our element. 2. It is comely; it is that which becomes us as reasonable creatures, much more as people in covenant with God. In giving honour to God we really do ourselves a great deal of honour. <div eID="gen13262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13263" type="x-p"/> II. God is recommended to us as the proper object of our most exalted and enlarged praises, upon several accounts. <div eID="gen13263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13264" type="x-p"/> 1. The care he takes of his chosen people, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.2">v. 2</reference>. Is Jerusalem to be raised out of small beginnings? Is it to be recovered out of its ruins? In both cases, <hi type="italic">The Lord builds up Jerusalem.</hi> The gospel-church, the Jerusalem that is from above, is of this building. He framed the model of it in his own counsels; he founded it by the preaching of his gospel; he adds to it daily such as shall be saved, and so increases it. He will build it up unto perfection, build it up as high as heaven. Are any of his people outcasts? Have they made themselves so by their own folly? He gathers them by giving them repentance and bringing them again into the communion of saints. Have they been forced out by war, famine, or persecution? He opens a door for their return; many that were missing, and thought to be lost, are brought back, and those that were scattered in the cloudy and dark day are gathered together again. <div eID="gen13264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13265" type="x-p"/> 2. The comforts he has laid up for true penitents, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.3">v. 3</reference>. They are <hi type="italic">broken in heart,</hi> and wounded, humbled, and troubled, for sin, inwardly pained at the remembrance of it, as a man is that is sorely wounded. Their very hearts are not only pricked, but rent, under the sense of the dishonour they have done to God and the injury they have done to themselves by sin. To those whom God heals with the consolations of his Spirit he speaks peace, assures them that their sins are pardoned and that he is reconciled to them, and so makes them easy, pours the balm of Gilead into the bleeding wounds, and then binds them up, and makes them to rejoice. Those who have had experience of this need not be called upon to praise the Lord; for when he brought them <hi type="italic">out of the horrible pit,</hi> and <hi type="italic">set their feet upon a rock,</hi> he <hi type="italic">put a new song into their mouths,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.40.2-Ps.40.3">Ps. xl. 2, 3</reference>. And for this let others praise him also. <div eID="gen13265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13266" type="x-p"/> 3. The sovereign dominion he has over the lights of heaven, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.4-Ps.147.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. The stars are innumerable, many of them being scarcely discernible with the naked eye, and yet he counts them, and knows the exact number of them, for they are all the work of his hands and the instruments of his providence. Their bulk and power are very great; but <hi type="italic">he calleth them all by their names,</hi> which shows his dominion over them and the command he has them at, to make what use of them he pleases. They are his servants, his soldiers; he musters them, he marshals them; they come and go at his bidding, and all their motions are under his direction. He mentions this as one instance of many, to show that <hi type="italic">great is our Lord and of great power</hi> (he can do what he pleases), and of <hi type="italic">his understanding there is no computation,</hi> so that he can contrive every thing for the best. Man's knowledge is soon drained, and you have his utmost length; hitherto his wisdom can reach and no further. But God's knowledge is a depth that can never be fathomed. <div eID="gen13266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13267" type="x-p"/> 4. The pleasure he takes in humbling the proud and exalting those of low degree (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord lifts up the meek,</hi> who abase themselves before him, and whom men trample on; but <hi type="italic">the wicked,</hi> who conduct themselves insolently towards God and scornfully towards all mankind, who lift up themselves in pride and folly, he <hi type="italic">casteth down to the ground,</hi> sometimes by very humbling providences in this world, at furthest in the day when their faces shall be <hi type="italic">filled with everlasting shame.</hi> God proves himself to be God by <hi type="italic">looking on the proud and abasing them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.40.12">Job xl. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen13267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13268" type="x-p"/> 5. The provision he makes for the inferior creatures. Though he is so great as to command the stars, he is so good as not to forget even the fowls, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.8-Ps.147.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. Observe in what method he feeds man and beast. (1.) <hi type="italic">He covereth the heaven with clouds,</hi> which darken the air and intercept the beams of the sun, and yet in them he <hi type="italic">prepareth</hi> that <hi type="italic">rain for the earth</hi> which is necessary to its fruitfulness. Clouds look melancholy, and yet without them we could have no rain and consequently no fruit. Thus afflictions, for the present, look black, and dark, and unpleasant, and we are in heaviness because of them, as sometimes when the sky is overcast it makes us dull; but they are necessary, for from these clouds of affliction come those showers that make the harvest to <hi type="italic">yield the peaceable fruits of righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.11">Heb. xii. 11</reference>), which should help to reconcile us to them. Observe the necessary dependence which the earth has upon the heavens, which directs us on earth to depend on God in heaven. All the rain with which the earth is watered is of God's preparing. (2.) By the rain which distils on the earth he <hi type="italic">makes grass to grow upon the mountains,</hi> even the high mountains, which man neither takes care of nor reaps the benefit of. The mountains, which are not watered with the springs and rivers, as the valleys are, are yet watered so that they are not barren. (3.) This grass he <hi type="italic">gives</hi> to <hi type="italic">the beast</hi> for <hi type="italic">his food,</hi> the beast of the mountains which runs wild, which man makes no provision for. And even the <hi type="italic">young ravens,</hi> which, being forsaken by their old ones, <hi type="italic">cry,</hi> are heard by him, and ways are found to feed them, so that they are kept from perishing in the nest. <div eID="gen13268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13269" type="x-p"/> 6. The complacency he takes in his people, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.10-Ps.147.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. In times when great things are doing, and there are great expectations of the success of them, it concerns us to know (since the issue proceeds from the Lord) whom, and what, God will delight to honour and crown with victory. It is not the strength of armies, but the strength of grace, that God is pleased to own. (1.) Not the strength of armies—not in the cavalry, <hi type="italic">for he delighteth not in the strength of the horse,</hi> the war-horse, noted for his courage (<reference osisRef="Job.39.19">Job xxxix. 19</reference>, &c.)—nor in the infantry, for he <hi type="italic">taketh no pleasure in the legs of a man;</hi> he does not mean the swiftness of them for flight, to quit the field, but the steadiness of them for charging, to stand the ground. If one king, making war with another king, goes to God to pray for success, it will not avail him to plead, "Lord, I have a gallant army, the horse and foot in good order; it is a pity that they should suffer any disgrace;" for that is no argument with God, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Ps. xx. 7</reference>. Jehoshaphat's was much better: <hi type="italic">Lord, we have no might,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.12">2 Chron. xx. 12</reference>. But, (2.) God is pleased to own the strength of grace. A serious and suitable regard to God is that which is, in the sight of God, of great price in such a case. The Lord accepts and <hi type="italic">takes pleasure</hi> in those that <hi type="italic">fear him and that hope in his mercy.</hi> Observe, [1.] A holy fear of God and hope in God not only may consist, but must concur. In the same heart, at the same time, there must be both a reverence of his majesty and a complacency in his goodness, both a believing dread of his wrath and a believing expectation of his favour; not that we must hang in suspense between hope and fear, but we must act under the gracious influences of hope and fear. Our fear must save our hope from swelling into presumption, and our hope must save our fear from sinking into despair; thus must we take our work before us. [2.] We must <hi type="italic">hope in God's mercy,</hi> his general mercy, even when we cannot find a particular promise to stay ourselves upon. A humble confidence in the goodness of God's nature is very pleasing to him, as that which turns to the glory of that attribute in which he most glories. Every man of honour loves to be trusted.
entries.93e1c714c9c489f7c06b7748abc21907a9470c98: <div eID="gen13269" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jerusalem and Zion Called to Praise to God; God's Favour to Israel.</title> <div sID="gen13270" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O Jerusalem; praise thy God, O Zion. 13 For he hath strengthened the bars of thy gates; he hath blessed thy children within thee. <hi type="super">14</hi> He maketh peace <hi type="italic">in</hi> thy borders, <hi type="italic">and</hi> filleth thee with the finest of the wheat. <hi type="super">15</hi> He sendeth forth his commandment <hi type="italic">upon</hi> earth: his word runneth very swiftly. <hi type="super">16</hi> He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes. <hi type="super">17</hi> He casteth forth his ice like morsels: who can stand before his cold? <hi type="super">18</hi> He sendeth out his word, and melteth them: he causeth his wind to blow, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the waters flow. <hi type="super">19</hi> He showeth his word unto Jacob, his statutes and his judgments unto Israel. <hi type="super">20</hi> He hath not dealt so with any nation: and <hi type="italic">as for his</hi> judgments, they have not known them. Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen13270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13271" type="x-p"/> Jerusalem, and Zion, the holy city, the holy hill, are here called upon to <hi type="italic">praise God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.147.12">v. 12</reference>. For where should praise be offered up to God but where his altar is? Where may we expect that glory should be given to him but in the beauty of holiness? Let the inhabitants of Jerusalem praise the Lord in their own houses; let the priests and Levites, who attend in Zion, the city of their solemnities, in a special manner praise the Lord. They have more cause to do it than others, and they lie under greater obligations to do it than others; for it is their business, it is their profession. "<hi type="italic">Praise thy God, O Zion!</hi> he is thine, and therefore thou art bound to praise him; his being thine includes all happiness, so that thou canst never want matter for praise." Jerusalem and Zion must praise God, <div eID="gen13271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13272" type="x-p"/> I. For the prosperity and flourishing state of their civil interests, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.13-Ps.147.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. 1. For their common safety. They had gates, and kept their gates barred in times of danger; but that would not have been an effectual security to them if God had not <hi type="italic">strengthened the bars of their gates</hi> and fortified their fortifications. The most probable means we can devise for our own preservation will not answer the end, unless God give his blessing with them; we must therefore in the careful and diligent use of those means, depend upon him for that blessing, and attribute the undisturbed repose of our land more to the wall of fire than to the wall of water round about us, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zech. ii. 5</reference>. 2. For the increase of their people. This strengthens the bars of the gates as much as any thing: <hi type="italic">He hath blessed thy children within thee,</hi> with that first and great blessing, <hi type="italic">Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the land.</hi> It is a comfort to parents to see their children blessed of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.9">Isa. lxi. 9</reference>), and a comfort to the generation that is going off to see the rising generation numerous and hopeful, for which blessing God must be blessed. 3. For the public tranquillity, that they were delivered from the terrors and desolations of war: <hi type="italic">He makes peace in thy borders,</hi> by putting an end to the wars that were, and preventing the wars that were threatened and feared. <hi type="italic">He makes peace within thy borders,</hi> that is, in all parts of the country, by composing differences among neighbours, that there may be no intestine broils and animosities, and <hi type="italic">upon thy borders,</hi> that they may not be attacked by invasions from abroad. If there be trouble any where, it is in the borders, the marches of a country; the frontier-towns lie most exposed, so that, if there be peace in the borders, there is a universal peace, a mercy we can never be sufficiently thankful for. 4. For great plenty, the common effect of peace: He <hi type="italic">filleth thee with the finest of the wheat</hi>—wheat, the most valuable grain, the fat, the finest of that, and a fulness thereof. What would they more? Canaan abounded with the best wheat (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.14">Deut. xxxii. 14</reference>) and exported it to the countries abroad, as appears, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Ezek. xxvii. 17</reference>. The land of Israel was not enriched with precious stones nor spices, but with <hi type="italic">the finest of the wheat,</hi> with bread, which strengthens man's heart. This made it the glory of all lands, and for this God was praised in Zion. <div eID="gen13272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13273" type="x-p"/> II. For the wonderful instances of his power in the weather, particularly the winter-weather. He that protects Zion and Jerusalem is that God of power from whom all the powers of nature are derived and on whom they depend, and who produces all the changes of the seasons, which, if they were not common, would astonish us. <div eID="gen13273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13274" type="x-p"/> 1. In general, whatever alterations there are in this lower world (and it is that world that is subject to continual changes) they are produced by the will, and power, and providence of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">He sendeth forth his commandment upon earth,</hi> as one that has an incontestable authority to give orders, and innumerable attendants ready to carry his orders and put them in execution. As the world was at first made, so it is still upheld and governed, by a word of almighty power. <hi type="italic">God speaks and it is done,</hi> for all are his servants. That word takes effect, not only surely, but speedily. <hi type="italic">His word runneth very swiftly,</hi> for nothing can oppose or retard it. As the lightning, which passes through the air in an instant, such is the word of God's providence, and such the word of his grace, when it is sent forth with commission, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.24">Luke xvii. 24</reference>. Angels, who carry his word and fulfil it, <hi type="italic">fly swiftly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.21">Dan. ix. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen13274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13275" type="x-p"/> 2. In particular, frosts and thaws are both of them wonderful changes, and in both we must acknowledge the word of his power. <div eID="gen13275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13276" type="x-p"/> (1.) Frosts are from God. With him are the <hi type="italic">treasures of the snow and the hail</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.22-Job.38.23">Job xxxviii. 22, 23</reference>), and out of these treasures he draws as he pleases. [1.] <hi type="italic">He giveth snow like wool.</hi> It is compared to wool for its whiteness (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Isa. i. 18</reference>), and its softness; it falls silently, and makes no more noise than the fall of a lock of wool; it covers the earth, and keeps it warm like a fleece of wool, and so promotes its fruitfulness. See how God can work by contraries, and bring meat out of the eater, can warm the earth with cold snow. [2.] <hi type="italic">He scatters the hoar-frost,</hi> which is dew congealed, as the snow and hail are rain congealed. This looks like ashes scattered upon the grass, and is sometimes prejudicial to the products of the earth and blasts them as if it were hot ashes, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.47">Ps. lxxviii. 47</reference>. [3.] <hi type="italic">He casts forth his ice like morsels,</hi> which may be understood either of large hail-stones, which are as ice in the air, or of the ice which covers the face of the waters, and when it is broken, though naturally it was as drops of drink, it is as morsels of meat, or crusts of bread. [4.] When we see the frost, and snow, and ice, we feel it in the air: <hi type="italic">Who can stand before his cold?</hi> The beasts cannot; they retire into dens (<reference osisRef="Job.37.8">Job xxxvii. 8</reference>); they are easily conquered then, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.20">2 Sam. xxiii. 20</reference>. Men cannot, but are forced to protect themselves by fires, or furs, or both, and all little enough where and when the cold is in extremity. We see not the causes when we feel the effects; and therefore we must call it <hi type="italic">his cold;</hi> it is of his sending, and therefore we must bear it patiently, and be thankful for warm houses, and clothes, and beds, to relieve us against the rigour of the season, and must give him the glory of his wisdom and sovereignty, his power and faithfulness, which shall not cease any more than summer, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.22">Gen. viii. 22</reference>. And let us also infer from it, If we cannot stand before the cold of his frosts, how can we stand before the heat of his wrath? <div eID="gen13276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13277" type="x-p"/> (2.) Thaws are from God. When he pleases (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.18">v. 18</reference>) <hi type="italic">he sends out his word and melts them;</hi> the frost, the snow, the ice, are all dissolved quickly, in order to which he <hi type="italic">causes the wind,</hi> the <hi type="italic">south wind, to blow,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the waters,</hi> which were frozen, <hi type="italic">flow</hi> again as they did before. We are soon sensible of the change, but we see not the causes of it, but must resolve it into the will of the First Cause. And in it we must take notice not only of the power of God, that he can so suddenly, so insensibly, make such a great and universal alteration in the temper of the air and the face of the earth (what cannot he do that does this every winter, perhaps often every winter?) but also of the goodness of God. Hard weather does not always continue; it would be sad if it should. He does not <hi type="italic">contend for ever,</hi> but <hi type="italic">renews the face of the earth.</hi> As he remembered Noah, and released him (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.1">Gen. viii. 1</reference>), so he remembers the earth, and his covenant with the earth, <reference osisRef="Song.2.11-Song.2.12">Cant. ii. 11, 12</reference>. This thawing word may represent the gospel of Christ, and this thawing wind the Spirit of Christ (for the Spirit is compared to the wind, <reference osisRef="John.3.8">John iii. 8</reference>); both are sent for the melting of frozen souls. Converting grace, like the thaw, softens the heart that was hard, moistens it, and melts it into tears of repentance; it warms good affections, and makes them to flow, which, before, were chilled and stopped up. The change which the thaw makes is universal and yet gradual; it is very evident, and yet how it is done is unaccountable: such is the change wrought in the conversion of a soul, when God's word and Spirit are sent to melt it and restore it to itself. <div eID="gen13277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13278" type="x-p"/> III. For his distinguishing favour to Israel, in giving them his word and ordinances, a much more valuable blessing than their peace and plenty (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.14">v. 14</reference>), as much as the soul is more excellent than the body. Jacob and Israel had God's statutes and judgments among them. They were under his peculiar government; the municipal laws of their nation were of his framing and enacting, and their constitution was a theocracy. They had the benefit of divine revelation; the great things of God's law were written to them. They had a priesthood of divine institution for all things pertaining to God, and prophets for all extraordinary occasions. No people besides went upon sure grounds in their religion. Now this was, 1. A preventing mercy. They did not find out God's statutes and judgments of themselves, but <hi type="italic">God showed his word unto Jacob,</hi> and by that word he made known to them his <hi type="italic">statutes and judgments.</hi> It is a great mercy to any people to have the word of God among them; for <hi type="italic">faith comes by hearing</hi> and reading that word, that faith without which it is impossible to please God. 2. A distinguishing mercy, and upon that account the more obliging: "<hi type="italic">He hath not dealt so with every nation,</hi> not with <hi type="italic">any</hi> nation; and, <hi type="italic">as for his judgments, they have not known them,</hi> nor are likely to know them till the Messiah shall come and take down the partition-wall between Jew and Gentile, that the gospel may be preached to every creature." Other nations had plenty of outward good things; some nations were very rich, others had pompous powerful princes and polite literature, but none were blessed with God's statutes and judgments as Israel were. Let <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">praise the Lord</hi> in the observance of these statutes. <hi type="italic">Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself to us, and not to the world! Even so, Father, because it seemed good in thy eyes.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.147"/> <div eID="gen13278" type="x-p"/>

entries.6d9df38fd01870dad106bbc17ce7e4ebc2df08a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7129"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 147</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.147.1-Ps.147.20">Psa 147:1-20</reference>. This and the remaining Psalms have been represented as specially designed to celebrate the rebuilding of Jerusalem (compare <reference osisRef="Neh.6.16">Ne 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.12.27">12:27</reference>). They all open and close with the stirring call for praise. This one specially declares God's providential care towards all creatures, and particularly His people.</title> <div sID="gen10932" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7129"/>1. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.92.1">Psa 92:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.135.3">135:3</reference>). <div eID="gen10932" type="x-p"/>

That power is put forth for the good of the meek and suffering pious, and confusion of the wicked (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.8">Psa 146:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.146.9">9</reference>). <div eID="gen10938" type="x-p"/>

Lord--</hi>literally, "Answer the Lord," that is, in grateful praise to His goodness, thus declared in His acts. <div eID="gen10940" type="x-p"/>

entries.d3840c6de574fab717d71f21c50f668c186ef527: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7140"/><div sID="gen10947" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7140"/>19-20. entries.4df9f4dc642972d761c7ea3d724aa56f216a346a: <div eID="gen23536" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23537" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23538" type="x-p"/> The psalmist praises God for his goodness to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.1-Psa.147.3">Psa 147:1-3</reference>; shows his great mercy to them that trust in him, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.4-Psa.147.6">Psa 147:4-6</reference>; he extols him for his mercies, and providential kindness, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.7-Psa.147.11">Psa 147:7-11</reference>; for his defense of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.12-Psa.147.15">Psa 147:12-15</reference>; For his wonders in the seasons, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.16-Psa.147.18">Psa 147:16-18</reference>; and his word unto Jacob, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.19">Psa 147:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.147.20">Psa 147:20</reference>. <div eID="gen23538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23539" type="x-p"/> This Psalm, which is without title in the Hebrew, Chaldee, and Vulgate, is attributed by the other Versions to Haggai and Zechariah. It was probably penned after the captivity, when the Jews were busily employed in rebuilding Jerusalem, as may be gathered from the second and thirteenth verses. It may be necessary to remark that all the Versions, except the Chaldee, divide this Psalm at the end of the eleventh verse, and begin a new Psalm at the twelfth. By this division the numbers of the Psalms agree in the Versions with the Hebrew; the former having been, till now, one behind. <div eID="gen23539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23540" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23541" type="x-p"/> Praise is comely - It is decent, befitting, and proper that every intelligent creature should acknowledge the Supreme Being: and as he does nothing but good to the children of men, so they should speak good of his name.
entries.da87b95a782925e55ec8b2ff5236591e31911e04: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23542" type="x-p"/> The Lord doth build up - The psalmist appears to see the walls rising under his eye, because the outcasts of Israel, those who had been in captivity, are now gathered together to do the work.
entries.26124e1219a4499ded559db04cd2f9882b325129: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23543" type="x-p"/> He healeth the broken in heart - שבורי, the shivered in heart. From the root שבר shabar, to break in pieces, we have our word shiver, to break into splinters, into shivers. The heart broken in pieces by a sense of God's displeasure.
entries.2ddcafd1b541262fe3ac23d6b0a68f9c0221b6d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23544" type="x-p"/> He telleth the number of the stars - He whose knowledge is so exact as to tell every star in heaven, can be under no difficulty to find out and collect all the scattered exiles of Israel.
entries.7e65097bb19c82e492e4c2bb9cebbe729f7cbbe9: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23545" type="x-p"/> His understanding is infinite - To his intelligence there is no number: though he numbers the stars, his understanding is without number. It is infinite; therefore, he can know, as he can do, all things.
entries.0138e4e2813f5de81e388e127b061ea1a3613dd2: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23546" type="x-p"/> The Lord lifteth up the meek - The humbled, the afflicted.
entries.b607f6a57f149036bd1a957fa69324ee63c5a908: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23547" type="x-p"/> Sing unto the Lord - ענו enu, sing a responsive song, sing in parts, answer one another.
entries.594a3470268d9ed568bd65620ab9e4daef121cd0: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23548" type="x-p"/> Who covereth the heaven with clouds - Collects the vapours together, in order to cause it to rain upon the earth. Even the direction of the winds, the collection of the clouds, and the descent of the rain, are under the especial management of God. These things form a part of his providential management of the world. <div eID="gen23548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23549" type="x-p"/> Maketh grass to grow upon the mountains - After this clause the Vulgate, the Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon, add, and herb for the service of man. It appears that a hemistich, or half-line, has been lost from the Hebrew text; which, according to the above Versions, must have stood thus: ועשב לעבדת האדם veeseb laabodath haadam, as in <reference osisRef="Psa.104.14">Psa 104:14</reference> : "And herbage for the service of mankind."
entries.9c9d33dbd9c465bb1a57e78671e4326d335363fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23550" type="x-p"/> He delighteth not - The horse, among all animals, is most delighted in by man for beauty, strength, and fleetness. And a man's legs, if well proportioned, are more admired than even the finest features of his face. Though God has made these, yet they are not his peculiar delight.
entries.db40c8f72781c3b6249589da8b01039430e2a14f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen23550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23551" type="x-p"/> The Lord taketh pleasure in them that fear him - That are truly religious. <div eID="gen23551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23552" type="x-p"/> In those that hope is his mercy - Who are just beginning to seek the salvation of their souls. Even the cry of the penitent is pleasing in the ear of the Lord. With this verse the hundred and forty-sixth Psalm ends in all the Versions, except the Chaldee. And the hundred and forty-seventh commences with the <reference osisRef="Psa.147.12">Psa 147:12</reference>. I believe these to be two distinct Psalms. The subjects of them are not exactly the same, though something similar; and they plainly refer to different periods.
entries.292129fc47b60552d0a7885ed9504a67d41b399d: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23553" type="x-p"/> He hath strengthened the bars of thy gates - He has enabled thee to complete the walls of Jerusalem. From the former part of the Psalm it appears the walls were then to progress; from this part, they appear to be completed, and provisions to be brought into the city, to support its inhabitants. The gates were set up and well secured by bars, so that the grain, etc., was in safety.
entries.719357d1f84ab59934fdbbcf11d7a97dbd12f6ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23554" type="x-p"/> He maketh peace - They were now no longer troubled with the Samaritans, Moabites, etc.
entries.6716ce424813b7ee2fbd083e15f2bb561d172e4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen23554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23555" type="x-p"/> He sendeth forth has commandment - His substantial word. It is here personified, מימרא meymra, Chaldee; and appears to be a very active agent running every where, and performing the purposes of his will.
entries.773b46ef199806916bf7df501a0e62b4923e6368: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen23555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23556" type="x-p"/> He giveth snow like wool - Falling down in large flakes; and in this state nothing in nature has a nearer resemblance to fine white wool. <div eID="gen23556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23557" type="x-p"/> Scattereth the hoar frost like ashes - Spreading it over the whole face of nature.
entries.8d67005a63869dc292c4cc1784d7417bc6db6f1b: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen23557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23558" type="x-p"/> He casteth forth his ice - קרחו korcho, (probably hailstones), like crumbs. <div eID="gen23558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23559" type="x-p"/> Who can stand before his cold? - At particular times the cold in the east is so very intense as to kill man and beast. Jacobus de Vitriaco, one of the writers in the Gesta Dei per Francos, says, that in an expedition in which he was engaged against Mount Tabor, on the 24th of December, the cold was so intense that many of the poor people, and the beasts of burden, died by it. And Albertus Aquensis, another of these writers, speaking of the cold in Judea, says, that thirty of the people who attended Baldwin 1: in the mountainous districts near the Dead Sea, were killed by it; and that in that expedition they had to contend with horrible hail and ice, with unheard-of snow and rain. From thls we find that the winters are often very severe in Judea; and in such cases as the above, we may well call out, "Who can stand against his cold!"
entries.f6f87aca5139d3f771f647ebcf33c7a2cf2bc6df: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen23559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23560" type="x-p"/> He sendeth out his word - He gives a command: the south wind blows; the thaw takes place; and the ice and snow being liquefied, the waters flow, where before they were bound up by the ice.
entries.10d1ea40009570d5570d2d4c2dfe3026ba267391: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen23560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23561" type="x-p"/> He showeth his word unto Jacob - To no nation of the world beside had God given a revelation of his will.
entries.49e2ff299e62b8dbb0113081a2d2d46bd65acff2: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen23561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23562" type="x-p"/> And as for his judgments - The wondrous ordinances of his law, no nation had known them; and consequently, did not know the glorious things in futurity to which they referred.  <chapter eID="Ps.147"/> <div eID="gen23562" type="x-p"/>

entries.1251c5e1ced5d7427fb2cb93c78a35104e264cca: <div eID="gen10333" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Hallelujah! Hallelujah to the Sustainer of All Things, the Restorer of Jerusalem</title> <div sID="gen10334" type="x-p"/> It is the tone of the restoration-period of Ezra and Nehemiah that meets us sounding forth out of this and the two following Psalms, even more distinctly and recognisably than out of the nearly related preceding Psalm (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.147.6">Psa 147:6</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.146.9">Psa 146:9</reference>). In Psalms 147 thanksgiving is rendered to God for the restoration of Jerusalem, which is now once more a city with walls and gates; in <reference osisRef="Ps.148.1-Ps.148.14">Psa 148:1-14</reference> for the restoration of the national independence; and in <reference osisRef="Ps.149.1-Ps.149.9">Psa 149:1-9</reference> for the restoration of the capacity of joyously and triumphantly defending themselves to the people so long rendered defenceless and so ignominiously enslaved. <div eID="gen10334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10335" type="x-p"/> In the seventh year of Artachshasta (Artaxerxes I Longimanus) Ezra the priest entered Jerusalem, after a journey of five months, with about two thousand exiles, mostly out of the families of the Levites (458 b.c.). In the twentieth year of this same clement king, that is to say, thirteen years later (445 b.c.), came Nehemiah, his cup-bearer, in the capacity of a <hi type="italic">Tirshâtha</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi>, p. 4). Whilst Ezra did everything for introducing the Mosaic Law again into the mind and commonwealth of the nation, Nehemiah furthered the building of the city, and more particularly of the walls and gates. We hear from his own mouth, in <reference osisRef="Neh.2.1">Neh 2:1</reference> of the Book that is extracted from his memoirs, how indefatigably and cautiously he laboured to accomplish this work. <reference osisRef="Neh.12.27">Neh 12:27</reference> is closely connected with these notes of Nehemiah’s own hand. After having been again in the meanwhile in Susa, and there neutralized the slanderous reports that had reached the court of Persia, he appointed, at his second stay in Jerusalem, a feast in dedication of the walls. The Levite musicians, who had settled down fore the most part round about Jerusalem, were summoned to appear in Jerusalem. Then the priests and Levites were purified; and they purified the people, the gates, and the walls, the bones of the dead (as we must with Herzfeld picture this to ourselves) being taken out of all the tombs within the city and buried before the city; and then came that sprinkling, according to the Law, with the sacred lye of the red heifer, which is said (<hi type="italic">Para</hi> iii. 5) to have been introduced again by Ezra for the first time after the Exile. Next the princes of Judah, the priests, and Levite musicians were placed in the west of the city in two great choirs (תּודת)<note placement="foot">The word has been so understood by Menahem, Juda ben Koreish, and Abulwalîd; whereas Herzfeld is thinking of hecatombs for a thank-offering, which might have formed the beginning of both festive processions.)</note> and processions (תּחלכת). The one festal choir, which was led by the one half of the princes, and among the priests of which Ezra went on in front, marched round the right half of the city, and the other round the left, whilst the people looked down from the walls and towers. The two processions met on the east side of the city and drew up in the Temple, where the festive sacrifices were offered amidst music and shouts of joy. <div eID="gen10335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10336" type="x-p"/> The supposition that <reference osisRef="Ps.147.1">Psa 147:1</reference> were all sung at this dedication of the walls under Nehemiah (Hengstenberg) cannot be supported; but as regards Psalms 147, the composition of which in the time of Nehemiah is acknowledged by the most diverse parties (Keil, Ewald, Dillmann, Zunz), the reference to the Feast of the Dedication of the walls is very probable. The Psalm falls into two parts, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.1-Ps.147.11">Psa 147:1-11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.12">Psa 147:12</reference>, which exhibit a progression both in respect of the building of the walls (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.2">Psa 147:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.13">Psa 147:13</reference>), and in respect of the circumstances of the weather, from which the poet takes occasion to sing the praise of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.8">Psa 147:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.16">Psa 147:16</reference>). It is a double Psalm, the first part of which seems to have been composed, as Hitzig suggests, on the appearing of the November rain, and the second in the midst of the rainy part of the winter, when the mild spring breezes and a thaw were already in prospect.
entries.104e13f53b3aaa2d5d6c70c53b6301f0178fe45d: <reference osisRef="Ps.147.1-Ps.147.6">Psa 147:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen10336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10337" type="x-p"/> The Hallelujah, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.135.3">Psa 135:3</reference>, is based upon the fact, that to sing of our God, or to celebrate our God in song (זמּר with an accusative of the object, as in Ps 30:13, and frequently), is a discharge of duty that reacts healthfully and beneficially upon ourselves: “comely is a hymn of praise” (taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.33.1">Psa 33:1</reference>), both in respect of the worthiness of God to be praised, and of the gratitude that is due to Him. Instead of זמּר or לזמּר, <reference osisRef="Ps.92.2">Psa 92:2</reference>, the expression is זמּרה, a form of the <hi type="italic">infin. Piel</hi>, which at least can still be proved to be possible by ליסּרה in Lev 26:18. The two כּי are co-ordinate, and כּי־נעים no more refers to God here than in <reference osisRef="Ps.135.3">Psa 135:3</reference>, as Hitzig supposes when he alters <reference osisRef="Ps.147.1">Psa 147:1</reference> so that it reads: “Praise ye Jah because He is good, play unto our God because He is lovely.” <reference osisRef="Ps.92.2">Psa 92:2</reference> shows that כּי־טוב can refer to God; but נעים said of God is contrary to the custom and spirit of the Old Testament, whereas טוב and נעים are also in <reference osisRef="Ps.133.1">Psa 133:1</reference> neuter predicates of a subject that is set forth in the infinitive form. In <reference osisRef="Ps.147.2">Psa 147:2</reference> the praise begins, and at the same time the confirmation of the delightful duty. Jahve is the builder up of Jerusalem, He brings together (כּנּס as in Ezekiel, the later wozd for אסף and קבּץ) the outcasts of Israel (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Isa 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.56.8">Isa 56:8</reference>); the building of Jerusalem is therefore intended of the rebuilding up, and to the dispersion of Israel corresponds the holy city laid in ruins. Jahve healeth the heart-broken, as He has shown in the case of the exiles, and bindeth up their pains (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.4">Psa 16:4</reference>), i.e., smarting wounds; רפא, which is here followed by חבּשׁ, also takes to itself a dative object in other instances, both in an active and (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Isa 6:10</reference>) an impersonal application; but for שׁבוּרי לב the older language says נשׁבּרי לב, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.19">Psa 34:19</reference>, Isa 61:1. The connection of the thoughts, which the poet now brings to the stars, becomes clear from the primary passage, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.26">Isa 40:26</reference>, cf. Isa 40:27. To be acquainted with human woe and to relieve it is an easy and small matter to Him who allots a number to the stars, that are to man innumerable (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">Gen 15:5</reference>), i.e., who has called them into being by His creative power in whatever number He has pleased, and yet a number known to Him (מנה, the <hi type="italic">part. praes</hi>., which occurs frequently in descriptions of the Creator), and calls to them all names, i.e., names them all by names which are the expression of their true nature, which is well known to Him, the Creator. What Isaiah says (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.26">Isa 40:26</reference>) with the words, “because of the greatness of might, and as being strong in power,” and (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.28">Isa 40:28</reference>) “His understanding is unsearchable,” is here asserted in <reference osisRef="Ps.147.5">Psa 147:5</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.145.3">Psa 145:3</reference>): great is our Lord, and capable of much (as in <reference osisRef="Job.37.23">Job 37:23</reference>, שׂגּיא כּח), and to His understanding there is no number, i.e., in its depth and fulness it cannot be defined by any number. What a comfort for the church as it traverses its ways, that are often so labyrinthine and entangled! Its Lord is the Omniscient as well as the Almighty One. Its history, like the universe, is a work of God’s infinitely profound and rich understanding. It is a mirror of gracious love and righteous anger. The patient sufferers (ענוים) He strengthens (מעודד as in <reference osisRef="Ps.146.9">Psa 146:9</reference>); malevolent sinners (רשׁעים), on the other hand, He casts down to the earth (עדי־ארץ, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.26.5">Isa 26:5</reference>), casting deep down to the ground those who exalt themselves to the skies.
entries.ab80a0e4c76bc0fe4e74cf3ffdf7d55b9a6e28ff: <reference osisRef="Ps.147.7-Ps.147.11">Psa 147:7-11</reference> <div eID="gen10337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10338" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Ps.147.7">Psa 147:7</reference> the song takes a new flight. ענה ל signifies to strike up or sing in honour of any one, Num 21:27; Isa 27:2. The object of the action is conceived of in בּתּודה as the medium of it (cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.16.4">Job 16:4</reference>). The participles in Psa 147:8. are attributive clauses that are attached in a free manner to לאלהינוּ. הכין signifies to prepare, procure, as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Job.38.41">Job 38:41</reference> - a passage which the psalmist has had in his mind in connection with Psa 147:9. מצמיח, as being the causative of a <hi type="italic">verb. crescendi</hi>, is construed with a double accusative: “making mountains (whither human agriculture does not reach) to bring forth grass;” and the advance to the thought that God gives to the cattle the bread that they need is occasioned by the “He causeth grass to grow for the cattle” of the model passage <reference osisRef="Ps.104.14">Psa 104:14</reference>, just as the only hinting אשׁר יקראוּ, which is said of the young of the raven (which are forsaken and cast off by their mothers very early), is explained from ילדיו אל־אל ישׁוּעוּ in Job <hi type="italic">loc. cit</hi>. The verb קרא brev ehT .tic .col boJ ni , κράζειν (cf. κρώζειν), is still more expressive for the cry of the raven, κόραξ, Sanscrit <hi type="italic">kârava</hi>, than that שׁוּע; κοράττειν and κορακεύεσθαι signify directly to implore incessantly, without taking any refusal. Towards Him, the gracious Sustainer of all beings, are the ravens croaking for their food pointed (cf. <reference osisRef="Luke.12.24">Luk 12:24</reference>, “Consider the ravens”), just like the earth that thirsts for rain. He is the all-conditioning One. Man, who is able to know that which the irrational creature unconsciously acknowledges, is in the feeling of his dependence to trust in Him and not in himself. In all those things to which the God-estranged self-confidence of man so readily clings, God has no delight (יחפּץ, pausal form like יחבּשׁ) and no pleasure, neither in the strength of the horse, whose rider imagines himself invincible, and, if he is obliged to flee, that he cannot be overtaken, nor in the legs of a man, upon which he imagines himself so firm that he cannot be thrown down, and which, when he is pursued, will presumptively carry him far enough away into safety. שׁוק, Arab. <hi type="italic">sâq</hi>, is the leg from the knee to the foot, from Arab. <hi type="italic">sâqa</hi>, root <hi type="italic">sq</hi>, to drive, urge forward, more particularly to urge on to a gallop (like <hi type="italic">curs</hi>, according to Pott, from the root <hi type="italic">car</hi>, to go). What is meant here is, not that the strength of the horse and muscular power are of no avail when God wills to destroy a man (Psa 33:16., Amo 2:14.), but only that God has no pleasure in the warrior’s horse and in athletic strength. Those who fear Him, i.e., with a knowledge of the impotency of all power possessed by the creature in itself, and in humble trust feel themselves dependent upon His omnipotence - these are they in whom He takes pleasure (רצה with the accusative), those who, renouncing all carnal defiance and self-confident self-working, hope in His mercy.
entries.9b1bee7a162e3c3f5cf513b155e30bb664310fc4: <reference osisRef="Ps.147.12-Ps.147.20">Psa 147:12-20</reference> <div eID="gen10338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10339" type="x-p"/> In the lxx this strophe is a Psalm (<hi type="italic">Lauda Jerusalem</hi>) of itself. The call goes forth to the church again on the soil of the land of promise assembled round about Jerusalem. The holy city has again risen out of its ruins; it now once more has gates which can stand open in the broad daylight, and can be closed and bolted when the darkness comes on for the security of the municipality that is only just growing into power (<reference osisRef="Neh.7.1-Neh.7.4">Neh 7:1-4</reference>). The blessing of God again rests upon the children of the sacred metropolis. Its territory, which has experienced all the sufferings of war, and formerly resounded with the tumult of arms and cries of woe and destruction, God has now, from being an arena of conflict, made into peace (the accusative of the effect, and therefore different from <reference osisRef="Isa.60.17">Isa 60:17</reference>); and since the land can now again be cultivated in peace, the ancient promise (Ps 81:17) is fulfilled, that God would feed His people, if they would only obey Him, with the fat of wheat. The God of Israel is the almighty Governor of nature. It is He who sends His fiat (אמרתו after the manner of the ויּאמר of the history of creation, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.33.9">Psa 33:9</reference>) earthwards (ארץ, the accusative of the direction). The word is His messenger (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.107.20">Psa 107:20</reference>), עד־מהרה, i.e., it runs as swiftly as possible, viz., in order to execute the errand on which it is sent. He it is who sends down snow-flakes like flocks of wool, so that the fields are covered with snow as with a white-woollen warming covering.<note placement="foot">Bochart in his <hi type="italic">Hierozoicon</hi> on this passage compares an observation of Eustathius on Dionysius Periegetes: τὴν χιόνα ἐριῶδες ὕδωρ ἀστείως οἱ παλαιοὶ ἐκάλουν.</note> <div eID="gen10339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10340" type="x-p"/> He scatters hoar-frost (כּפור from כּפר, to cover over with the fine frozen dew or mist as though they were powdered with ashes that the wind had blown about. Another time He casts His ice<note placement="foot">lxx (Italic, Vulgate) κρύσταλλον, i.e., ice, from the root κρυ, to freeze, to congeal (Jerome <hi type="italic">glaciem</hi>). <hi type="italic">Quid est crystallum?</hi> asks Augustine, and replies: <hi type="italic">Nix est glacie durata per multos annos ita ut a sole vel igne acile dissolvi non possit</hi>.</note> (קרחו from קרח; or according to another reading, קרחו from קרח) down like morsels, fragments, כפתּים, viz., as hail-stones, or as sleet. The question: before His cold - who can stand? is formed as in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.6">Nah 1:6</reference>, cf. Psa 130:3. It further comes to pass that God sends forth His word and causes them (snow, hoar-frost, and ice) to melt away: He makes His thawing wind blow, waters flow; i.e., as soon as the one comes about, the other also takes place forthwith. This God now, who rules all things by His word and moulds all things according to His will, is the God of the revelation pertaining to the history of salvation, which is come to Israel, and as the bearer of which Israel takes the place of honour among the nations, Deu 4:7., 32-34. Since the poet says מגּיד and not הגּיד, he is thinking not only of the Tôra, but also of prophecy as the continuous self-attestation of God, the Lawgiver. The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> דּבריו, occasioned by the plurals of the parallel member of the verse, gives an unlimited indistinct idea. We must keep to דברו, with the lxx, Aquila, Theodotion, the Quinta, Sexta, and Jerome. The word, which is the medium of God’s cosmical rule, is gone forth as a word of salvation to Israel, and, unfolding itself in statutes and judgments, has raised Israel to a legal state founded upon a positive divine law or judgment such as no Gentile nation possesses. The Hallelujah does not exult over the fact that these other nations are not acquainted with any such positive divine law, but (cf. Deu 4:7., Baruch 4:4) over the fact that Israel is put into possession of such a law. It is frequently attested elsewhere that this possession of Israel is only meant to be a means of making salvation a common property of the world at large.  <chapter eID="Ps.147"/> <div eID="gen10340" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 147
This Psalm also incites the people of God to praise him upon two accounts; first, for the display of his power, goodness, wisdom, and other perfections in the common government of the world, and the several parts of it, the heavens and the earth, but more particularly for his special goodness in cherishing and defending the Church which he has chosen of his free grace, in restoring it when fallen down, and gathering it when dispersed.
In the Hebrew text, and in the Chaldee and Vulgate versions, this Psalm is without a title, but in the Septuagint it is assigned to the days of Haggai and Zephaniah, the title being — Αλλελουια Αγγαιου και Ζαχαριου; and this may be regarded as a probable reference. In Psalm 147:2 and Psalm 147:13 there seems to be an allusion to the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Bishop Horsley entitles it — “Thanksgiving of the returned captives. Perhaps composed for a Pentecost or Feast of Trumpets, after the Restoration.” “Eben Ezra, and other Jewish writers, think that it foretells the future rebuilding of Jerusalem, and the restoration of the Jews from their present captivity, and refer it to the times of Messiah.” — Dr. Gill.
Psalm 147:1-6
1. Praise ye God; for it is good to sing praises unto our God, for it is pleasant, and praise is comely. 2. Jehovah building up Jerusalem, will gather the dispersed of Israel: 3. Healing the contrite in heart, and binding up their griefs: 4. Numbering the multitude of the stars, giving names to each of them. 5. Great is our Lord, and plenteous in power, there is no figure for his understanding. 6. Jehovah raiseth up the miserable, and casteth the wicked down to the ground.
 
Praise ye God, etc. Though the benefits he speaks of are such as God extends to all men indiscriminately, it is plain that he addresses more especially God’s people, who alone behold his works in an enlightened manner, whereas stupidity and blindness of mind deprive others of their understanding. Nor is his subject confined to the common benefits of God, but the main thing which he celebrates is his mercy, as shown to his chosen people. That the Church may address itself to the praises of God with more alacrity, he states that this kind of exercise is good, delightful, and pleasant, by which he indirectly censures a sin which is all but universal of becoming wearied at the very mention of God, and counting it our highest pleasure to forget both God and ourselves, that we may give way to unrestrained indulgence. To teach men to take a delight in this religious exercise, the Psalmist reminds them that praise is comely, or desirable. For the term נאוה, navah, may be rendered either way.
